By transforming the coordinates into linear differential operators in a commuting momentum space, we can reformulate this issue into an ordinary quantum problem. These operators, representing the coordinates $\hat{x}_i$, have associated eigenfunctions that satisfy the commutation relations $[\hat{x}_i,\hat{x}_j]=if_{ij}^{\;\;\;k}X_k$. In a given Lie algebra associated with the structure constants, we can choose the basis $X_i$ such that the corresponding unitary operators $\hat{U}_i$ either bound the spectrum into discrete values (compact algebras) or yield the spectrum's spectrum values (noncompact algebras). This allows us to solve the Schrödinger equation for a particle in a noncommutative space by solving an ordinary quantum problem associated with a commuting Lie algebra, whether it be compact or noncompact.

Determining atmospheric properties needs a sufficient and representative set of photometric data from stars, an extensive understanding of light path interaction with optical properties of the atmosphere, as well as a capacity to conduct precise photometry under varying atmospheric conditions. Unfortunately, few groups in China have successfully carried out reliable atmospheric corrections due to the lack of sufficient data from comparison stars, especially in highly variable seeing conditions such as near sunrise or sunset. As an effort to tackle this challenge near the Yunnan Observatories, we outline several key points for successful comparison star selection, including the necessity of at least ten times as many exposure images as needed data points for correction, as well as the preference for red stars in sunset and blue stars in sunrise to minimize scattering effects. Our research revealed that in this environment, it is inevitable that occasional long streaks of adversarial actions will occur more frequently than one might expect. yzed coherent states (SPCCSs) can be generated via quantum-optical catalysis using beam splitters or parametric amplifiers. These states occur when a coherent state and a single-photon state interact in two input ports, and a catalyzed photon appears in a third output port. Our research into SPCCSs considers their structural properties, state transformations under specific optical processes, and their experimental realizations. Notably, we demonstrate that SPCCSs possess unique characteristics such as nonclassicality, quantum interference, and quantum superposition. Our results also show that SPCCSs possess desirable qualities like self-sufficiency, self-compression, and self-amplification. By utilizing the Heisenberg uncertainty principle and quantum fluctuation analysis, our work establishes that SPCCSs can be self-amplified without diminishing their nonclassical nature. Furthermore, we prove that SPCCSs can be self-compressed via a SQUID protocol when the catalytic mode exhibits stronger squeezing than the signal and idler modes, as well as when using a beam splitter with higher transmissivity than reflectivity. Our research indicates that SPCCSs can be self-amplified through the application of a beam splitter with higher transmissivity than reflectivity, and their self-amplified state exhibits both increased mean photon number and stronger quantum fluctuations than their initial state.

Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are primarily centered on enhancing target target user experiences by leveraging source domain user interactions. Nevertheless, such strategies are limited by their reliance on user profiles and fail to effectively leverage rich item content to prevent suboptimal recommendations. To tackle these limitations, we introduce UserItem-aware Dual-domain Necessity-aware Collaborative learning (UIDNCL), a novel user-item aware dual-domain necessity-aware collaborative learning framework for multi-domain collaborative filtering. UIDNCL partially aligns dual-user latent space sources and targets by minimizing their dual-norm distance, dynamically adapting the alignment degree based on user's domain necessity. Furthermore, it performs dual-norm attention to identify particularly source-necessary and target-necessary users. UIDNCL partially aligns dual-item content space sources and targets in a similar manner. Finally, UIDNCL integrates dual-user Item attention to pinpoint necessary items from both domains by fusing their sources and targets items attention. Three public benchmarks demonstrate that UIDNCL consistently surpasses state-of-the-art models in recommendation accuracy and recall. Notably, UIDNCL also exhibits remarkable robustness in target domain sparse scenarios and outperforms other models even under a sparse target domain data setup. The open-sourced code of UIDNCL is available at https://github.com/zhengqian1999/UserItem-aware-Dual-domain-Necessity-aware-Collaborative-learning-.

Different object detectors exploit scene context for recognition using various methods.
However, most of these methods only consider global context.
Ignoring local context around the object limits their performance.
To address this issue, we propose a novel network named CR-NET.
This network divides the image into separate branches, with one branch extracting object features and another extracting local context features.
An innovative network named R²GNet is used for feature extraction from both the main object branch and the context branch.
These features are then combined through a contextual attention mechanism.
We evaluate CR-NET with two popular detectors named YOLOv2 and SSD.
Our method significantly improves the mean average precision by 5% to 12% and reduces the loss function value by 15% to 25%,
demonstrating the effectiveness of incorporating local context in detection.

Based on the LAT data alone, we identified six extremely rare, cosmic-ray scale, ultra-high energy photons with energies ranging from 316 MeV to 316 GeV that originated from a burst of $\gamma$-rays. However, based on data from multiple wavelength bands, including $\gamma$-rays from the Fermi/GBMT, X-rays from the Neil Telescopes and the Swift/XRT, and the Lyot $\alpha$ ray, only one of these LAT photons can be associated with the primary LAT direction within the measurement error margin of 2°. Given the LAT photons' energy requirements that exceed the pair conversion threshold from traditional models, a new explanation is needed. To address this, possible UHE photon generation mechanisms are discussed and their pair conversion effects are examined. The resulting late-time LAT photon spectrum derived from the initial LAT photons shows a cutoff at 100 MeV, assuming the LAT photons are produced by the synchrotron process from ultra-high energy electrons with a power-law distribution of $n = 3$.

Gravitational lensing of quasar pairs, first theorized in 1986, was observed for the first time in 2019 and offers a new cosmological parameter, the Hubble constant ($H_0$), to be determined with systems beyond 150 megaparsecs. We simulate the velocity distribution pattern of two stars formed by a lensing system by using quasar A2237+0312 as a reference, and the result is that such systems will exhibit a distinct localized maximum in their probability distribution, unlike the Gaussian distribution pattern seen with standard binary star systems. We introduce a comprehensive end-to-end neural network model and learning method in the context of support vector machines. The newly proposed end-to-end structure utilizes an $l_2$-norm norm for vector length calculation, an $\epsilon$-outlier robust threshold, and fully learnable non-negative projection matrices. In contrast to traditional SVM applications with $l_2$ norms and thresholds using $l_1$ or $l_\infty$ norms, our design addresses different issues. We evaluate the effectiveness of our end-to-end structure for both classification and anomaly detection tasks. For classification, the use of $l_2$-norm makes it challenging for the model to converge using standard optimization algorithms like cross-entropy loss functions. In order to address this challenge, we introduce an efficient learning method termed as $\epsilon$-robust threshold optimization that enables stable and rapid convergence. In order to demonstrate the effectiveness of our structure, we apply it to multiple datasets for classification tasks, as well as for both classification and outlier detection. For classification and outlier detection, the model achieves superior performance compared to existing end-to-end models.

Next,  we'll cover the essential frameworks like floating base dynamics and rigid body constraints that define the problem.  Then,  we'll explore our solution, which utilizes a continuous hybrid systems approach consisting of discrete decisions and continuous dynamics.  Specifically,  we'll detail our method that employs impact-aware periodic model predictive control, highlighting how we separate the cost function and feasibility terms into gait and transition components.  We adopted a 1DoF half-full model to develop gait patterns efficient in computational processing.  Moreover,  we implemented a neural network to predict gait residuals real-time,  reducing the frequency of dynamic iterations while maintaining high accuracy.  Finally,  we'll reveal how we ensure stable and robust behavior through a 2-second-horizon MPC that adapts to disturbances and external forces within computationally feasible time. as an unknotting operation. It can be demonstrated that any knot diagram can be converted into a trivial unknot through a sequence of unknotting operations, combined with some variations in the diagram configuration, which are referred to as Reidemeister moves. Unknotting operations hold significant value in the field of knot theory, not only aiding in both research and teaching, but also serving as an essential step in certain knot invariants calculations, such as the Jones polynomial. Moreover, they are involved in several transformation algorithms, including the tetrahedralization of knots. However, traditional unknotting operations take quite some time to execute, notably affecting the length, complexity, and even the topological characteristics of the remaining knot. In our research, we introduce a novel unknotting operation called the surgery move, which is derived from the concept of surgery on knots. This new move is shown to preserve certain knot properties, such as knot quaternions and their associated quaternions, and also results in a quicker reduction of the aforementioned parameters. Moreover, we prove that any knot diagram can indeed be transformed into a trivial unknot through a sequence of surgery moves, and notably, this can be accomplished with a stricter upper bound on the resulting parameter values.

We examine the potential role of amplitude-based effective field theories (EFTs) in this plan. This review begins with the fundamental concepts of EFTs in quantum field theory, including their application to colliders, the representation of interactions using helicity amplitude methods, and the systematic development of higher-order corrections. The advantages of helicity-based EFT constructions in terms of computational efficiency are highlighted. We then discuss specific cases where we have achieved significant reductions in computational resources, such as cutting memory usage in half or improving it by an order of magnitude, while maintaining comparable speed to traditional methods. These findings demonstrate that using helicity methods with EFTs can be highly effective, with the potential for substantial gains in both speed and memory management as the number of involved particles increases, a factor that will be especially critical for future colliders. This review is complemented by available C++ and Fortran tools that can be readily integrated into the pipeline of upcoming experiments.

tetralogy of Fallot patients requires accurately predicting when the heart chamber will become over-expanded. Traditionally, this prediction is based on left ventricular end-diastolic area from echocardiograms. However, these 2D measurements lack precision due to the complex shape of the heart chamber. In this study, we take a more accurate approach by using magnetic resonance imaging to generate a detailed 3D model of the heart chamber. These models were validated against existing ultrasound measurements. We then developed and tested a new method involving implicit surface reconstruction to create precise 3D models of pulmonary artery aneurysms, establishing the end-diastolic volume as 54.3 ± 19.5 ml/m^2, nearly 2 times as accurate as the traditional area measurement. By combining CT and MRI scans, we produced even more precise models with surface errors of just 1.8 ± 0.7 mm. By utilizing magnetic resonance imaging to create individualized 3D models, surgeons can have more reliable information about their patients' conditions and make better-informed decisions on the timing of valve replacement surgery.

Pyramid Networks (FPNs), frequently struggle with identifying large-scale objects due to an inherent drawback in the framework. This paper reexamines FPN within the context of detection systems and sheds light on its success factors. We identify three critical issues with FPNs: (1) an insufficient number of channel features; (2) ineffective feature fusion methodology; and (3) insufficient high-frequency information. To tackle these limitations, we introduce three pivotal modifications: (1) an innovative feature pyramid structure that leverages feature interactions; and and (2) a top-down upsampled channel enhancement module that integrates feature maps; and (3) parallel network architecture that incorporates multi-scale feature memory to supplement high-frequency information. Comprehensive experimental evaluation on the COCO and MS COCO datasets confirms that the proposed modified FPN not only rectifies errors that impact precision on large-scale object identification but also enhances overall performance by enhancing recall on small-scale objects.

In contrast, this paper delves into a micro-level analysis, where the removal of individual nodes during an attack is examined in detail. Based on percolation theory, the authors analyze the effects of removing a single node that causes other nodes to disconnect from the main component. By applying this micro-level approach to a random attack on a Cayley tree network, the distribution of the resulting node removal sizes is derived.

The direct discovery of cosmic X-ray bursts and pulsars relies heavily on the precise identification of powerful gamma-ray bursts triggered by violent cosmic events. Furthermore, these rare high-energy cosmic occurrences must compete with intense gamma-ray background radiation, significantly decreasing the detector's sensitivity. To rectify these challenges, a novel method involving the entanglement of photons has been proposed for both detector schemes. By utilizing a specially designed non-linear crystal to generate a state of single-mode squeezed vacuum from a long-wavelength illuminating photon, we can reduce power fluctuations and enhance sensitivity, allowing for two-way communication via entangled photons using the same powerful illuminating laser. This innovative technique paves the way for more effective gravitational wave detection, direct gamma-ray burst detection, and the observation of cosmic X-ray bursts and pulsars.

As a result of their large size, MIMO arrays are subject to spatially correlated small-scale fading effects that are often oversimplified as negligible. A more accurate model involves a latent factor model that takes into account a random diagonal matrix to account for signal components perpendicular to the antenna surface. In this study, we propose a novel random matrix theory (RMT) framework for analyzing precoding strategies in large-scale MIMO systems with spatially correlated fading. We specifically examine the performance of multiuser beamforming by calculating the mean and variance of signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratios (SINRs). Our research establishes that, in certain configurations, SINR fluctuations become negligible, allowing for accurate performance predictions of MIMO system throughput. The derived results are validated through computer simulations that confirm their accuracy. Furthermore, we analyze the effectiveness of MRMT in evaluating the throughput of MIMO systems using different precoding methods, including multiuser beamforming, full beamforming, and coherent combining.

electrolyte interphase (SEI) in the context of electrochemical energy storage, with various approaches being employed to examine its properties and composition. Techniques like spectroscopy, microscopy, and theoretical modeling have yielded valuable insights, yet often provide only partial information due to their limitations. We propose a novel method to combine an X-ray based technique, specifically Seitz source code, to simulate and analyze the composition and structural properties of a detailed SEI model, leveraging previously obtained experimental data to create a comprehensive "virtual material" representation. This, in turn, allows us to accurately predict key compositional and structural properties, offering a framework for a more holistic understanding of the SEI's physical behavior. We apply this method to an SEI formed on a graphite anode, an critical interface in many electrochemical energy storage systems, and accurately reproduce experimental observations, including anomalous X-ray scattering behavior, anomalous X-ray emission, changes in the open circuit voltage, anomalous X-ray absorption, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy spectra, X-ray standing wave depth profiling, and transmission electron microscopy images. Our comprehensive "virtual material" approach, capable of describing the complex and heterogeneous SEI interface, is an invaluable tool in the search for novel electrolytes and binders, specifically in the context of electrochemical energy storage systems, where it is becoming increasingly important.

-carbon power grids is expected to be energy communities. These decentralized groups of consumers who generate their own power are motivated by environmental concerns as well as personal incentives to collaborate. We develop an optimization model for a multi-year energy planning horizon where the grid operator sets the rules of collaboration, including pricing policies. The energy community then reacts to these incentives in a game theoretic manner. Our approach combines an integer linear programming model for the community's intra-year planning with a collaborative game, where the operator optimizes for social welfare while allowing the community to act in its own interests. We test this framework on a real-world scenario in southern Germany and find that it can lead to significant utility gains for the community without harming overall welfare. The findings highlight the potential of our approach to facilitate the adoption of collaborative energy projects in real-world applications.

from being trained using the maximum-likelihood principle, but this is problematic when applying them to non-i.i.D. data, as it can cause a model to overfit and become overly sensitive to label noise. This issue can be mitigated by applying a non-MLE principle that promotes invariance to data distribution shifts. One common non-MLE approach is to employ a prototype network to learn typical feature representations for each class and update the main network to minimize the distance between class prototypes and its classifications. However, this approach often results in the prototypes becoming too tight and containing outliers, which can lead to the same problem as training with MLE. In contrast to this approach, we instead aim to expand the prototypes to better fit the data and propose a new objective function that minimizes the distance between the prototypes and the mean features most similar to the prototypes rather than the mean features of each class. This objective function promotes invariance to data distribution shifts while maintaining good classification performance, as evidenced by experimental results on multiple benchmark datasets using both clean and noisy labels.

detected the production of top quarks for the first time using proton-lead data at an 8.16 TeV nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy. Recent work has proven the effectiveness of using non-cooperative game models, such as Stackelberg games, to analyze the concurrent transmission problem. This research delves deeper into concurrent transmission game analysis by determining the value of the reflective component's influence through a metric called game utility. Built upon weighted Stackelberg strategies, this study proposes a framework to maximize the utility of all participants within the communications network, resulting in a more robust and reliable communication system with a higher rate of successful transmissions characterized by a higher utility value.

Sketch employs randomized linear measurements to map vectors into a lower-dimensional space, particularly effective at identifying the top elements (with the largest squared magnitude) of a given vector. However, the CountSketch sketch falls short in situations where subsequent vectors rely on adaptation based on previously identified top components. This limitation makes it highly susceptible to persistent bias when applied to data streams. As a result, the performance degrades dramatically when analyzing up to $k$ largest components of dense vectors or sparse vectors with high non-zero per element. In comparison to techniques based on covariance matrices and their equivalents, CountSketch-based methods lag far behind, requiring roughly an order of magnitude larger data sets ($\tilde{O}(d/k)$ vs. $\tilde{O(\sqrt{d/k})}$ for dense vectors and $\tilde{O(sparsity/\sqrt{dk})}$ vs. $\tilde{O(\sqrt{d/k})}$ for sparse vectors). Even a straightforward alternative to the CountSketch sketch known as CountSketch with Clipping outperforms the traditional CountSketch by several orders of magnitude in performance.

In this context, compact objects can emerge from the system, giving birth to exotic compact binaries or even transient point sources of optical, X-ray, or gravitational wave emissions. Diverse configurations can be found within these CE systems. However, most of them remain concealed and unseen during this phase, with their final outcomes solely revealed through compact object mergers. We propose an alternative end to these systems featuring rapidly rotating massive stars instead, with the internal friction-generated energy causing the envelope to radiate and shed, eventually resulting in a stellar ejection. Our detailed radiative hydrodynamic simulations explore various rotating hypergiant configurations with high friction rates, exhibiting rapid envelope radiation shedding over decades or even centuries with blue continuum or even UV continuum line emissions attractive to observational study. We contend that some systems might be masquerading as active high binary star candidates, with their true nature as CE systems approaching revelation through careful observation.

we studied a distant starburst galaxy, examining how star formation-driven gas outflows are linked to other properties of the galaxy. Our data show a nearly linear relationship between outflow mass and star formation rates, as well as a significant correlation between outflow mass and gas usage times. In regions of high star formation rates within the galaxy, the mass ejected through outflows actually exceeds the amount of gas converted into new stars, indicating a limit on how quickly gas can be turned into stars due to outflows. Our findings when analyzing groups of entire galaxies are consistent with these results, but the relationship between outflow mass and gas usage times there is on the threshold of being statistically significant. We propose that the strong relationship we observe between outflows and gas dynamics in starburst galaxies may offer crucial insights for understanding the regulation of star formation in galaxies at early stages of development.

time-dependent partial differential equations involves preserving inherent properties of the original solution. Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques, including validating existing schemes' preservation properties and proposing innovative methods achieving both high accuracy and property preservation. Although such schemes, when paired with implicit time-stepping methods, ensure preservation of certain properties, they unfortunately result in high computational costs comparable to increasing the spatial discretization precision. In contrast to these methods, we present an explicit construction of a divergence-free numerical solution for time steps, yielding a stable, precise, and preservation-friendly scheme for the heat equation. This scheme employs only one order of computational expense per time step, thus allowing for the use of large time steps without compromising stability. As such, it enables divergence control through temporal methods, a differing approach to traditional divergence-controlling methods that primarily modify spatial discretizations or apply post-processing to numerical solutions.

motion trajectories for specific points within an animated three-dimensional environment. Motion trajectory data has been found beneficial for downstream tasks like activity classification and navigation within applications such as autonomous driving. Nevertheless, obtaining accurate motion data poses a challenge due to difficulties in annotation and the absence of clear depth information in video data, especially when the scene is dynamic. Currently, most methods either rely on noisy instance segmentation masks or estimate rough depth, which degrades motion accuracy. To address these issues, we propose a technique that projects the instance segmentation mask onto the depth buffer, allowing the point cloud to be segmented simultaneously with more precise depth and boundary details. Building upon this, we introduce a motion-aware instance segmentation technique that leverages motion cues within the instance mask to accurately predict scene motion. Experimentally, our method achieves remarkable motion accuracy on the synthetic KITTI dataset and outperforms baseline methods on both synthetic and real-world datasets. Additionally, we incorporate this technique into downstream navigation and classification models, where the integrated motion awareness notably enhances their performance.

However, their ability to provide guaranteed performance bounds or intuitive insights into their behavior is limited. To address this, we propose utilizing fractional linear programs (LFPs) as guiding approximations for deep learning machine functions, an area that has not been extensively explored. Our key contribution is an innovative proof showing the applicability of LFPs to artificial neural systems configurations. These systems, given an arbitrary number of hidden layers, can be proven to perform optimally with LFPs, which in turn enables several beneficial applications. Specifically, we can establish performance bounds for neural systems, whether trained using stochastic gradient descent or any other method. Additionally, LFPs enable us to derive novel rates of artificial neural function differentiation, enabling the analysis of time-varying parameters and inputs. These systems, given a limited number of hidden layers, layers of fractions and differences, and artificial neural growth functions, can be evaluated in polynomial time. Our research aims to explore the relationship between cubic graphs and 3-edge-colourings to identify those whose every perfect matching corresponds to a colour of the graph's edge-colouring. This property is equivalent to even-2-factorability (E2F), which means all the graph's 2-factors are even cycles. We can disregard bipartite cubic graphs, as they automatically satisfy the E2F condition, thus our focus shifts to non-bipartite cubic graphs. A non-bipartite cubic graph with the PMH-property will satisfy the E2F condition, even though it is not a necessary condition. Our work involves introducing the papillon graph, an infinite family of E2F non-bipartite cubic graphs parameterized by two values. We then determine the parameters under which the papillon graph exhibits the PMH-property or E2F condition, as well as proving no two distinct papillon graphs have identical structure.

To facilitate this process, WiFi fingerprinting, a technique where features from WiFi signal readings from a target's location are mapped, has been widely adopted. Notably, a phenomenon known as the cluster effect arises from the fluctuations in WiFi signal measurements, causing the creation of overlapping regions in the feature space and potentially leading to inaccurate positioning results. To address this issue, we propose a new position estimation approach, termed CLoVER, which leverages the characteristics of the cluster effect and defines a cluster-based target class in the feature space. A key issue in these studies is that traditionally, theoretical calculations use a single, uniform interaction to determine energy levels, disregarding the unique properties of individual nucleons and their energy states. This is because it's challenging to generalize the effects of short-range correlations, which typically cause a shift and distortion in energy states. As a result, there's a persistent error in predicted binding energies that hasn't been addressed for quite some time. In this study, we address this issue by incorporating the effects of short-range correlations through a new approach to shift and modify single-particle energy states, rather than treating it as a constant. When particles encounter potential barriers thicker than their de Broglie wavelength, they experience exponential attenuation, which can be significantly influenced by local environmental factors near the barrier. A nearby electromagnetic field or lattice vibrations have substantial effects on tunneling attenuation, with potential barriers having an irregularly increasing threshold and external forces potential having a decreasing increase. Consequently, this could lead to competing effects resulting in weak or no dependence of tunneling current on barrier thickness. To investigate this, we modeled tunneling as a function of barrier thickness with both resistance and lattice vibrations taken into account using an external AC field model. Our study revealed a quantum tunneling minimum size below which tunneling current no longer decreases with increased barrier width. This minimum size is determined primarily by the Wigner time constant, associated with the tunneling path length, and is only minimally affected by near-barrier lattice vibrations. Near the critical radius, we could potentially utilize tunneling diodes to filter electrons based on their de Broglie wavelength.

Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy (LITT) treats seizures caused by epilepsy in a specific brain area. Researchers at Fudan University analyzed volumetric MRI images from healthy control subjects and epilepsy patients before and after a laser treatment. The study used advanced image processing techniques to track changes in the brain's structure and blood flow, comparing the results to similar studies in other conditions. The findings showed that the treatment created an elliptical-shaped lesion in the epileptic brain region without significant changes to the surrounding white matter tracts. This research highlights the therapeutic effects of LITT, setting the stage for developing more effective treatment plans through the use of AI-based methods.

A study has analyzed the extent of tree-based ancestor states in the context of graph states with graph connectivity represented as a star or path in a complete graph of N qubits. A dynamic framework by nature, this method eliminates several of the mass-flux convection scheme's assumptions that are no longer valid at modern model resolution levels. Nonetheless, the optimal approach for solving the multi-fluid equations in relation to atmospheric convection remains unclear. The present paper outlines a simple single-column two-fluid model featuring ascending and descending fluid components with the exclusion of additional sub-filter variation modeling. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating useful patterns while rejecting unnecessary details. The effectiveness of the Co-Imitation Learning framework is verified through extensive experiments in simulated pick-and-place tasks and a real mobile robot exploration scenario.

Moreover, obtaining such detailed labels from radiologists is time-consuming and costly.  To overcome these challenges, we developed a novel weak supervision technique called JSONIE that leverages unstructured clinical reports.  This approach automates the extraction of relevant information from reports and uses it to train models with high accuracy.  Unlike previous methods based on sentence-level annotations, JSONIE focuses on capturing relationships between objects in the clinical report.  As a result, it allows objects to have multiple conflicting labels without needing to resolve them.  To handle this issue, we used mutual learning to integrate these results and demonstrate its benefits over previous methods through experimental results.  Additionally, we showed that JSONIE works effectively across multiple datasets and modalities, outperforming baseline methods on tasks such as microvascular complications, cardiovascular risk factors, and bone age assessment in X-ray images.  Our work is made available to the public at https://github.com/jeffhsw/JSONIE.

Recent studies have developed various approaches to identify these patterns, yet they often struggle with a key challenge: comprehensively exploring the underlying causes of unusual dynamics. To tackle this issue, we propose an innovative method called Unsupervised Reinforcement Learning with Natural Language Processing (UReNLP) to investigate complex systems. By leveraging supervised sequence-to-sequence models and reinforcement learning, our approach enables a comparative analysis of typical and atypical behavior while examining both local and global impacts. As a demonstration, we apply UReNLP to analyze neural activity during an epileptic seizure, uncovering its underlying structure and significance within a comparative and multi-scale framework. We further validate the method on two additional datasets: stock market data and an agent-based economic model. The findings reveal that the neural activity can be viewed as a negative reinforcement learning problem and introduce a new concept, 'policy disruption,' for better understanding of unusual events in complex systems.

A specific subset of potential properties is studied which comprise generalized Hermite polynomials, constructed through the use of Wronskians from standard Hermite polynomials, often seen in mathematical physics and random matrix theory. This potential property uses two inputs: one dependent on time and another fixed. A graph can be created to depict the relationship between these inputs, and this construction leads to dynamic Sturm-Liouville operators that describe the probability distribution of orthogonal polynomial ensembles at fixed time steps. The analysis also reveals conditions and formulas for when generalized Hermite polynomials are orthogonal, as well as identifies monodromy-free conditions for matrix-valued Schrödinger operators. A theorem is presented that offers sufficient conditions, based on the structure of the associated graph, guaranteeing that these operators are monodromy-free, as well as identifying an equivalent system of algebraic differential equations.

Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Within this revised framework, the article provides solutions to Menger's initially posed problems.

Our findings show a significant disparity, up to an order of magnitude, between the results obtained from these two frameworks due to differing approaches in handling final-state parton showers. We also discover that the limits set by the data on total cross sections, as well as other processes such as Higgs boson production, are less constrained, exhibiting up to 30% variation when including final-state parton showers and a more significant impact from other non-perturbative effects such as heavy flavor production and hadronization.

Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radar systems that utilize direct digital synthesis and digital down-conversion. This approach is applied under both filtered and unfiltered conditions through Monte Carlo simulations.

The compatibility operator can be parameterized by the original differential operator when a specific non-degeneracy condition is met. A novel method is presented to address this parameterization. magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have motivated the investigation of the effect's influence on the dynamics of domain wall motion. From the anomalous Hall effect formula, it is known that the term responsible for this phenomenon is linearly proportional to the magnetization. Consequently, we anticipate that the anomalous Hall voltage within a domain will be directly proportional to the square of the domain's width. When an in-plane domain wall is driven by the Hall effect and the magnetization within the central wide domain and domain interface behaves as Gdn2 (where d is the domain wall coordinate), we observe a unique scenario in which the total Hall force acting on the domain wall is unresponsive to domain wall width variations. Our numerical simulations further corroborate this finding, demonstrating that oscillating domains of any initial width will remain stable over time.

Our analysis revealed that the pandemic's effect on monthly real GDP growth was overwhelmingly negative, with a one percentage point decline in real GDP growth associated with each additional COVID-19 infection. interlayer tunneling models were the primary theoretical frameworks used to explain the complex phenomenon of high-temperature cuprate superconductivity. Although both theories could account for the within-plane properties of cuprates, their ability to do so was due to an unforeseen fortuitous cancellation of contrary effects. Our work reveals that a boson condensation theory for d-wave superconductivity yields straightforward and direct consequences of high symmetry planes within the BZ. These consequences include the expected observation of a distinct magnetic field direction dependency in the critical current within the d-wave cuprates. Furthermore, our model provides the necessary conditions for the tunneling voltage to be proportional to the square of the chemical potential and the tunnel conductance to be a function of the square of the applied voltage. Consequently, these phenomena have readily testable implications.

two-dimensional solitons, like those for Bose-Einstein condensates described by the Gross-Pitaevskii equations, have the property of Galilean invariance. This allows for solitons to be moved from a stationary state by incorporating invariance. Researchers face a challenge in finding models capable of exhibiting stable, self-accelerating motion of solitons. Self-accelerating modes of light fields can be represented by parabolic equations that bear resemblance to the Schrödinger equation. In one dimension, the existence of stable self-accelerating solitons has been called into question due to issues with the associability of associated power flows. Here we present two types of one-dimensional Bose polarons which exhibit self-accelerating motion in the form of paraxial bright-polariton condensates known as polaritonscats. These models are based on the modified Gross-Pitaevskii equations that include linear and nonlinear effective masses for the atomic components. We demonstrate that these systems can support self-accelerating solitons that carry finite power flows in both linear and nonlinear masses.

A real-world scenario for this approach could involve an image classification system trained for traffic light interpretation that unexpectedly encounters multiple target domains, each characterized by unique lighting conditions, orientations of the traffic lights, and environments such as streets, construction sites, and warehouses. To test our hypothesis, we utilized the Amazon dataset of images of appliance boxes without labels, creating six different domains influenced by varying degrees of noise. We then developed two methods for identifying these diverse target domains unsupervisedly and experimented with two classification frameworks to evaluate their effectiveness. The outcomes demonstrate that our technique successfully detects two of the six target domains and when combined with a contrastive learning framework yields promising outcomes.

Thanks to advancements in microscopy and the ability to study samples over billions of years, paleo-detectors can potentially offer cost-effective searches for dark matter across a vast parameter space. Using analysis, the likelihood of paleo-detectors can offer the most cost-effective search for WIMPs, capable of achieving a sensitivity to a recoil energy of 1 eV and a mass of 10 GeV to 1 TeV, an order of magnitude better than current methods. Furthermore, the design flexibility of paleo-detectors allows for the ability to search for different types of dark matter with varying masses using existing rocks across the globe.

a nano-Hertz gravitational wave background signal remains elusive in current data. Nevertheless, enhanced datasets are expected to yield statistically significant evidence in the future. This study endeavors to eliminate sampling bias in data analysis by utilizing exhaustive likelihood methodology. Building upon this comprehensive framework, an enhanced nested sampling technique has been developed for implementing Bayesian inference. The results of our exhaustive likelihood analysis verify the statistical significance of nano-Hertz gravitational wave signals in simulated datasets representing next-generation pulsar timing array experiments. The analysis demonstrates that, with an enhanced dataset of ~10 years' worth of simulated data comprising 14 virtual pulsars, significant evidence at over 5-sigma can be achieved in about 30% of realizations. This level of significance in simulations mirrors the anticipated outcomes for PPTA and NANOGrav moderate datasets of ~6-7 years' worth of data with up to ~11 down-conversion frequencies per timing baseline. Furthermore, our analysis provides an optimized Bayesian technique that surpasses previously reported nested sampling results in terms of computational efficiency by a factor of ten.

The problem of characterizing training data and its effects on the model's performance and output is unexplored comprehensively. Our work proposes a novel framework to map out the output space of machine learning models, identifying regions with similar features in the interior of the convex hull of the training dataset. These regions are called Data Dominant Regions (DDRs). We introduce two metrics to quantify the shape and quality of DDRs: the Region Map Metric (RMM) and the Data Dominance Metric (DDM). Specifically, we define the RMM and Data Dominant Regions (DDRs) using support vector regression (SVMR), and the DDM and DDRs are calculated via $k$-means (KDDM). Ultimately, our research contributes a systematic method for mapping the training data and the model's output in the context of supervised learning.

For example, if one agent has a random policy while the others are more skilled, existing offline methods can't distinguish between inter-agent strategy differences and naturally occurring variability in experiences, potentially misidentifying the optimal strategy as less effective. However, the development of quantum information science has since enabled the verification of these variables' impossibility through quantum tripartite correlations, involving at least three parties. However, the widespread adoption of LSTMs has been hindered by their intricate internal workings, which significantly impedes our ability to understand their underlying mechanisms. This research aims to enhance our comprehension of LSTMs by comparing their functional characteristics with a simpler theoretical model called the Rational Memory Network (RMN). Through an analytical framework, we examined the LSTMs' behavior from both a signal processing and information storage perspective, and our results reveal that LSTM cells with a positive forget gate effectively mimic RMN networks under certain conditions. Moreover, we found that LSTMs can be understood as combining recurrent rational memory networks through this analytical approach. Our study not only facilitates the development of more interpretable LSTM alternatives with improved performance, such outperforming LSTM on multiple benchmarks, but also provides insights for designing future deep recurrent neural models by illuminating their design principles and internal structures.

We utilize Monte Carlo simulations to investigate the phase diagram resulting from these interactions, and our findings are compared with the performance of a minimum-weight perfect matching decoder. This research provides a method for assessing the fundamental error thresholds of quantum error correcting codes, independently of any specific decoding strategies, and could help inform the design of near-term quantum computing hardware.

To address this, we develop simplified formulas to estimate when droplets will settle based on their initial size, temperature and humidity levels and without considering precipitation's Precipitation impact. GPU and TPU advancements in recent years, can be summarized using Peter Shor's famous speedup formula from Shor's 1994 paper, which showed that quantum algorithms offer a significant speedup over classical ones by converting polynomial-time tasks into linear-time tasks, specifically for integer factorization. This can be seen as a two-step process: first, reducing a task with extensive overhead to a more straightforward task with less extra work, and then accelerating slow steps from a slower to a faster time frame. In this work, we present an alternative quantum algorithm that can factor integers in linear time with a more efficient step size, resulting in a logarithmic subroutine instead of a quadratic one, and providing a direct solution to the problem without following the two-step process. This can be achieved by applying a large jump and then making finer adjustments to pinpoint the exact answer, which can be applied to other mathematical problems that have distinct components that are unique to a given input and in a specific function.

in wide-field X-ray monitors employing lobster-eye (LE) optics, we propose a concept called multiplexed lobster-eye (MuLE) optics. The simulation showed that the MuLE optics can be effective in determining the source's location with a 64-pixel sensor, provided that additional data from previous observations is used to help pinpoint the rotation angle of each mirror section.

Our approach decomposes the 4-dimensional equilibrium equations into three key components: conservation of mass and momentum in 3-dimensional rotating coordinates, the Barotropic equation, and an exact non-linear map linking specific enthalpy to mass density. By formality reducing the hydrodynamic equations, we derive conditions that our solution must satisfy, effectively transforming the problem into a way to determine the rotational angular velocity curve of the star. Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation holds significant potential to further our understanding of neutron star events. We examine how specific pairs of gravitational waves and photons can provide constraints on the equation of state of neutron star matter. In particular, we propose using a Bayesian framework to place rigorous limits on a series of physically meaningful parameters, which include maximum neutron star mass, neutron star radius, and minimum binary separation at the time of merger. We also demonstrate the methodology with an example of GW190425, which represents a merging binary neutron star event withChandra X-ray Telescope data providing no significant emission. We anticipate this approach to be applicable to future events detected in the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA collaboration run 3 and beyond.

The (6,6)CNT-pyCrx systems exhibit a unique geometry where the carbon atoms of the carbon nanotube and the pyridine ring coexist on the same spherical surface.  The localization of Cr 3d d-orbitals leads to a robust magnetic moment in these systems, with (6,6)CNT-pyCrx displaying half-integer spins and exhibiting metallic behavior.  However, adding more pyridine molecules causes the emergence of a delocalized p$\pi$ orbital, which hybridizes with the Cr d-orbitals and induces a spin polarization in the pyridine ring.  Our findings, validated by a tight-binding model, reveal that (6,6)CNT functionalized with magnetic and non-magnetic groups exhibits rich magnetic properties driven by the competition between magnetic and non-magnetic groups.

Our results illustrate that this dense gas network is generally parallel to the galactic plane, although in the inner 400 parsecs of the CMZ it appears to align more closely with the galactic longitudes of $\pm$ 330 deg, where it may act as a structural support system in this complex region. As the galactic longitudes move away from the CMZ's edge, the network's spatial arrangement is represented as a function of gas column density and velocity relative to the Local Standard of Rest. These observations suggest that the linear structures are most prominent in lower density areas and where the gas is dragged into the CMZ by the gravitational pull of the central bulge. Additionally, the possible presence of long-lived orbital resonances, such as the ILR or CMZ-BAR, could be contributing to the formation of this intricate network.

Initially, we investigated the generation of highly polarized electrons using a classical approach and found that their spinning motion could reach extreme values of billions radians per second. It is proposed that this mechanism could serve as an indicator of this type of magnetic field in other stars as well.

The study delves into the structure of vector field and one-form bundles on stacks formed from groupoids, establishing results similar to those found in their smooth manifold counterparts. It establishes the existence of dual one-form bundles and establishes a relationship between the total one-form bundle and the tangent bundle. It establishes a correspondence between non-degenerate differential forms on stacks and symplectic structures on these spaces. It examines Stokes' Theorem and establishes a relationship between Lie algebroids and their dual constructions. continuum cores from the Dragon 7 starless core revealed an anisotropic structure composed of perpendicular filaments, which deviates from the fractal nature observed in other sub-millimeter continuum observations of starless cores. These filaments can be differentiated based on a mass-power law rather than length, and this filterability holds until a size of approximately 1000 AU, beyond which the anisotropic organization likely results from gas pressure effects rather than maintaining a specific power-law dimensionality. Depending on the mass distribution within a cluster, filaments may be observed as dense strands connecting low-mass stars or merged into a single structure connecting high-mass stars. Although the anisotropic filamentary pattern in Dragon 7 does not yet indicate a direct link to the observed low-mass protostars, it may influence their spatial distribution. Moreover, an energy balance calculation based on the filamentary structure in Dragon 7 suggests a possible self-fractalizing process that balances at around 1000 AU, where the energy input from small-scale turbulence balances radiative cooling losses, which could result in anisotropic filaments around low-mass protostars through a self-fractalizing process.

an extension of intutionistic modal logics with prelinearity. This study explores algebraic and relational semantics for Godel modal logics built upon the duality between finite Godel algebras and finite forests, a type of poset. The research considers subvarieties of basic Godel algebras with two modal operators, alongside their respective classes of forest frames, both with single and double accessibility relations. These relational structures serve as prelinear counterparts to traditional intuitionistic modal logic semantics. The study specifically examines two expansions of finite Godel algebras: the addition of Dunn axioms, common in positive classical and intutionistic logic, and the addition of Fischer Servi axioms. The research provides Jonsson-Tarski-like representation theorems for different types of finite Godel modal algebras with operators.

To address this issue, we introduce a novel approach to correcting the accuracy of depth sensor data by leveraging a small set of labeled 3D points. Our method starts with optimizing the transformation parameters of the point clouds to align them with their global coordinates. Next, we identify and remove outlier points using a two-stage process. While several assessments have been developed to measure curiosity in various populations, there's a gap in the availability of validated tools to evaluate scientific curiosity in high school students in Iran. This study's objective was to create and examine scientific curiosity assessment items for this demographic. Three expert panels consisting of 15 education specialists, two psychology experts, and 15 science education experts reviewed and refined 54 initial items down to 29. A total of 750 high school students participated in a survey to evaluate the refined 29 items, which were subsequently reduced through exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis to 18 common factors accounting for a significant 70.8% of the variance in curiosity scores. Examining the reliability of the 29 items through Cronbach's alpha and composite reliability methods yielded impressive results of .979 and .943, respectively. The core concept of MFSSA involves representing continuous multivariate functions within a specific core domain and executing a technique akin to multivariate functional principal component analysis through deterministic decomposition. AR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves. A plasma source with a 0.1 meter length and 0.4 meter diameter provides plasma necessary for the experiment, and features a helical antenna to produce high-density plasma in the helicon mode of discharge. Until now, it was unclear if this plasma source could achieve helicon mode, which is essential for it to function effectively. A study was conducted to verify this capability, involving detailed plasma parameter calculations and experimental evidence. It was found that the plasma source can indeed operate in helicon mode, confirmed by a increase in plasma density at higher coil currents. To further enhance its capabilities, the input power was upgraded to 13 kW, resulting in higher plasma parameters that support its use in the ICRF test facility.

Various intracellular pathways trigger pyroptosis, with ubiquitination playing a significant role by attaching ubiquitin molecules to target proteins. al Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. gravity theory can be transformed through specific equivalences, where it's equivalent to a theory of cosmological constant and topological terms, including Chern-Simons theory in both its gauge and Lie algebra forms. This equivalence forms the foundation of a new quantum gravity approach in three dimensions, where the original theory's parameters are quantized as part of a path integral. This method's application to AdS3 space leads to a partition function that depends on two sl(2,R) groups' Chern-Simons theory, in both its gauge and Lie algebra forms, with parameters defined by the original theory's coupling and cosmological constant. Integrating this combined theory's bulk quantities over a manifold with a boundary results in both discrete and continuous terms in the partition function. Notably, the continuous term's coefficient is related to a special value of the Riemann zeta function. This outcome aligns with previous findings in Cardy's formula and Brown-Henneaux central charges in theory. The quantity obtained can be interpreted in terms of Chern-Simons levels and dual conformal field theory central charges in both sl(2,R) groups.

The order of these sequences may be independent and identically distributed (IID), or it may exhibit non-IID characteristics.  This paper proposes a two-stage procedure to estimate the total of interest.  First, a estimator from Borchardt et al.  is used to produce an initial estimate.  If this estimate diverges from zero,  the procedure either terminates or incorporates additional samples.  The latter option has the advantage of not requiring the sample interval size to be known in advance.  Two methods to supplement the initial sample are suggested.  The first involves a basic block of additional samples that can be adjusted based on the performance of the initial estimator.  The second approach suggests a small number of small additional samples that are adaptively obtained in response to the initial estimator.  The size and order of these additional samples do not affect the variance estimate's consistency.  When additional sample information is available,  the variance estimate can potentially be substantially reduced.  Numerous simulated experiments demonstrate the accuracy of the proposed method in various scenarios, including when the initial sample consists of non-IID data.  The proposed method was also used to estimate the total number of unregistered voters in a specific city.

Traditionally, THz communication is confined to short-distance applications because THz signals face high absorption in the atmosphere. To overcome this limitation, researchers have explored the potential of multi-hop directional transmission techniques to extend THz communication range in acyclic network topologies. However, these studies have not yet considered the practical challenges of implementing such networks with bidirectional links that are necessary for heterogeneous network scenarios. In this paper, we address this research gap by formulating a THz multi-hop transmission problem for bidirectional star-shaped graph networks, where multiple groups of multi-hop routes are necessary. Moreover, these routes must provide equitable service to all users and ensure that at least one return path is available for each forward transmission. Furthermore, we consider the challenge of feasible THz beam alignment that satisfies equity among users. Due to the interdependence of THz beam alignment and route selection, this problem becomes highly complex, and existing solution methods are ineffective. To address this, we developed an innovative algorithm called FairEquityMultiGraphBeamSearch to generate multiple THz simultaneous route alignments that are equitable among users in bidirectional star-shaped graph networks.

for calculating electromagnetic multipoles: Cartesian primitive multipoles, irreducible multipoles and spherical multipoles. Our findings suggest that the spherical multipoles provide the most accurate description of electromagnetic interactions, as demonstrated by their ability to correctly predict results from simple physical systems. These systems include two-atom models that mimic real crystals with dielectric responses, and various three-atom arrangements that exhibit resonant dipole-quadrupole-quadrupole forces, retarding dipole-quadrupole forces, and magnetoelectric forces. For other functions like Gaussian distributions this direct approach doesn't apply but a potential transformation to a convex coordinate system restores efficiency. This paper investigates such a method for dense overlapping normal distributions of equal width sigma centered at regular square lattice points with unit spacing sigma^2 times sigma times the square of pi over four with finite outer radius R and unit normal orientation over the plane of the lattice points by initially converting the normal distribution function to a shifted Dirac delta function with an additive constant and evaluating the Dirac delta function over the lattice points before computing the constant term using the area of the region and normal distribution. This efficient square lattice method is compared to an outstanding result in gravitational physics using hierarchical octree points in three-dimensional space oriented normally over the plane with three-dimensional region obtained by integrating over the normal coordinate of the distribution function.
